items.summary:
of Oxford, draws on disciplines including computer science, philosophy, and sociology. The latest report offers a sweeping look at where AI stands today and where it may be headed. [...] Risks once dismissed as futuristic speculation are materializing. AI agents have broken out of secure testing environments and accessed external systems without authorization. The line between near-term ethical concerns (such as algorithmic bias) and longer-term existential risks is blurring, and the report warns that the rapid, poorly regulated deployment of today's most powerful systems is accelerating that convergence.

## Governance Lacks Consensus [...] International AI governance remains fragmented, increasingly shaped by national security framing rather than global cooperation. Export controls, chip restrictions, and competitive pressures between the U.S. and China have turned AI into an instrument of geopolitical rivalry. While high-level summits have produced statements of principle, the report concludes they have fallen short of meaningful, enforceable commitments, even as publics worldwide call for stronger regulation.

Without the restriction on x in the original function, it wouldn't have had an inverse function: 3 + sqrt[(x+5)/2] [...] Now, that last example is not to be said it can't be done, but it involves completing the square to obtain f(x) = (x-2)2+2, then inversing it so that you get f -1(x) = 2-sqrt(x-2).

However, there is another way that doesn't rely so much on informality and will work whether or not you can figure out exactly what you did with exactly one x. [...] On this last function, the implied domain of the inverse is [0,1). That means that the range of the original function must have been [0,1), also. Check it on your calculator, and you'll see it is.

items.summary:
Now it is time to explore the graphs of functions and their inverses further. Use the quadratic function f(x) = x2 restricted to the domain 0, ∞) so that it is one-to-one, and graph it as in figure 5.

 y=x^2 

Quadratic function with domain restricted to [0, ∞) [...] (input of the original function), then the “inverse” is not a function at all! To put it differently, the quadratic function is not a one-to-one function; it fails the horizontal line test, so it does not have an inverse function. In order for a function to have an inverse, it must be a one-to-one function. [...] From the other side of the same problem, starting with the square (parent quadratic) function f(x) = x2. There is a problem creating the inverse, because for every given output of the quadratic function, there are two corresponding inputs (except when the input is 0). For example, the output 9 from the quadratic function corresponds to the inputs 3 and −3. items.title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure | WIRED
items.summary: The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written," Chaudhuri says. “There’s a middle ground.” [...] Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one [...] More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

items.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5: Accelerating Physical Intelligence — Google DeepMind
items.summary: Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks. [...] Using our embodied reasoning model (Gemini Robotics ER) to keep track of the workflow, and the Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model to control its hands and arms, the robot reaches into supply bins, picks up metal automotive brackets, and places them into sequencing containers, all while correcting for any gaps. Achieving a 96% success rate, this pilot shows promising progress toward widespread real-world industrial applications. [...] Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses inference-time reasoning guidance to steer around physical hazards in real-time. Much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Gemini’s responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%.
